claim: RBM7 expression positively correlates with overall survival of breast cancer patients in TCGA, GEO and METABRIC datasets.
source: Analysis of TCGA, GEO and the METABRIC breast cancer datasets showed that RBM7 expression positively correlates with overall survival of breast cancer patients (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: Supported by analysis of multiple patient datasets (TCGA, GEO, METABRIC) and referenced figures showing survival curves.

claim: RBM7 low expression predicts reduced disease-free survival in patients with breast cancer.
source: RBM7 low expression predicts the reduced disease-free survival in patients with breast cancer (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by survival analysis data shown in referenced figures.

claim: RBM7 is decreased in breast cancer compared to normal tissues.
source: Congruently, we found RBM7 is decreased in breast cancer compared to normal tissues (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by expression analysis data comparing tumor and normal tissues shown in figures.

claim: Cases with lymph node metastasis have lower expression of RBM7 compared to cases without metastasis.
source: Further dissection in a cohort of breast cancer patients from the cBioPortal unveiled cases with lymph node metastasis have lower expression of RBM7 as compared to cases without metastasis (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by analysis of cBioPortal patient cohort data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Patients bearing clinical stage III tumors have significantly decreased RBM7 expression than patients bearing I and II clinical stage tumors.
source: The results showed that patients bearing clinical stage III tumors have significantly decreased RBM7 expression than patients bearing I and II clinical stage tumors (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data on tissue microarrays shown in Figure 1E.

claim: RBM7 exhibits reduced protein levels in triple negative breast cancer tumors compared to paracancer tissues.
source: In tissue chip containing triple negative breast cancer, the more aggressive and mesenchymal breast cancer subtype, RBM7 exhibits reduced protein levels in tumors as compared to paracancer tissues (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data on tissue microarrays shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Most primary tumor samples displayed positive IHC staining for RBM7, whereas most lung/liver metastatic lesions showed weak or negative RBM7 expression.
source: Most (25% strong positive;67% moderate positive) of primary tumor samples displayed a positive IHC staining for RBM7, whereas most of lung/liver metastatic lesions showed weak or negative RBM7 expression (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry analysis of 21 primary cancer and 9 metastatic samples shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The expression of RBM7 is significantly decreased in lymph node metastases compared to corresponding primary tumors.
source: We also obtained paired primary breast cancer and lymph node metastatic loci and found, when compared to the corresponding primary tumor, the expression of RBM7 is significantly decreased in lymph node metastases (Figure 1H–I).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data on paired samples shown in Figures 1H-I.

claim: Differentially expressed genes upon RBM7 knockdown were enriched in extracellular matrix organization, cell migration and angiogenesis.
source: Strikingly, Gene Ontology and pathway analysis displayed a wide range of differentially expressed genes were enriched in extracellular matrix organization, cell migration and angiogenesis (Figure 2A–B), which have been characterized as crucial processes in tumor metastasis.
evidence: Supported by Gene Ontology and pathway analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figures 2A-B.

claim: Metastasis-associated genes were up-regulated upon RBM7 knockdown in breast cancer cells.
source: We then conducted qRT-PCR analysis of theses metastasis-associated genes in RBM7-depleted breast cancer cells and verified that they were up-regulated upon RBM7 knockdown shown as heatmap representation (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR validation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: RBM7-silenced 4T1 cells developed more spontaneous lung metastases than control cells in BALB/c mice.
source: RBM7-silenced 4T1 cells were able to develop more spontaneous lung metastases than control cells as judged by pulmonary nodules number and haematoxylin-eosin (HE) staining of lung tissues (Figure 2D–F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by in vivo tail-vein transfer model data shown in Figures 2D-F.

claim: The depletion of RBM7 led to a visible increase in mobility and invasiveness of breast cancer cells.
source: We utilized transwell chamber with or without matrix coat and would healing assays to examine the potential function of RBM7 in migration and invasion capabilities and found the depletion of RBM7 led to a visible increase in mobility and invasiveness of both the triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) cell line MDA-MB-231, estrogen receptor positive breast cancer cell line MCF7 and 4T1 cells (Figure 2G–H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-E).
evidence: Supported by transwell and wound healing assay data shown in Figures 2G-H and supplementary figures.

claim: RBM7 overexpression notably repressed MDA-MB-231 and MCF7 cells migration and invasion.
source: Conversely, RBM7 overexpression notably repressed MDA-MB-231 and MCF7 cells to migrate or invade across transwell inserts (Figure 2I–J).
evidence: Supported by transwell assay data with RBM7 overexpression shown in Figures 2I-J.

claim: HUVEC incubated with culture medium from RBM7-knockdown breast cancer cells exhibited accelerated tube formation.
source: Compared to the scramble control, HUVEC incubated with culture medium from RBM7-knockdown breast cancer cells exhibited accelerated tube formation length and branch junction (Figure 2K), suggesting the inhibitory effect of RBM7 on breast cancer angiogenesis.
evidence: Supported by tube formation assay data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Almost 551 splicing events occurred significant decrease in PSI upon RBM7 ablation, whereas 289 splicing events endured increased PSI.
source: Intriguingly, we observed that, attributed to the ablation of RBM7, almost 551 splicing events occurred significant decrease in PSI (percent spliced in), whereas 289 splicing events endured increased PSI (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis of alternative splicing events shown in Figure 3A.

claim: SE (skipping exon) events were the most prominently regulated type of alternative splicing by RBM7.
source: The changed events were divided among various types of AS (alternative splicing), including SE (skipping exon), IR (intron retention), A5E (alternative 5' splice site exon), A3E (alternative 3' splice site exon), and MXE (mutually exclusive exons), of note, SE events were the most prominently regulated (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by categorization of alternative splicing events from RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A majority of AS events in particular of SE and A5E category were in decrease of PSI upon RBM7 depletion.
source: A majority of AS events in particular of SE and A5E category were in decrease of PSI upon RBM7 depletion (Figure 3C–D), indicating that the presence of RBM7 may promote the usage of alternative splice sites of SEs or A5Es.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figures 3C-D and logical inference about RBM7 function.

claim: UUUCUU motif, similar to RBM7 binding site (polyU), were enriched in RBM7 positively regulated AS events to a greater extent than control exons unimpacted by RBM7.
source: Subsequently, we extracted the candidate binding motifs which reside within or near cassette exons or A5E and found UUUCUU motif, simiar to RBM7 binding site (polyU) were enriched in RBM7 positively regulated AS events to a greater extent that control exons unimpacted by RBM7 (Figure 3E), raising the possibility that RBM7 may serve as a splicing activator through directly tethering cis-element in pre-mRNA.
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3E and inference about RBM7 mechanism.

claim: RBM7 exhibits nuclear localization in breast cancer cells.
source: This is coherent with the nuclear localization of RBM7 in breast cancer cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The PSI of selected genes related to cancer progression was either increased or decreased endogenously upon RBM7 depletion.
source: The RT-PCR analysis demonstrated that the PSI of selected gene related to cancer progression was either increased or decreased endogenously upon RBM7 depletion (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR validation data shown in Figure 3F and supplementary figure.

claim: A majority of genes undergoing AS alterations were involved in cytoskeleton assembly and organization.
source: Gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis identified a majority of genes undergoing AS alterations were involved in cytoskeleton assembly and organization (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: RBM7-regulated downstream splicing events are functionally connected to well-linked network containing gene subgroups associated with biological processes in tumor cell metastasis.
source: While globally analyzing the network enrichment of RBM7-regulated downstream splicing events, we observed its targets are functionally connected to well-linked network containing gene subgroups (Figure 3H), which are associated with biological processes in tumor cell metastasis, again suggesting the cancer-related function of RBM7.
evidence: Supported by network enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3H and inference about cancer relevance.

claim: MFGE8 was identified as a hub gene by overlapping RBM7 RIP-seq data, RNA-seq data with RBM7 knockdown, and alternative splicing analysis.
source: To ascertain the functional targets that explain the inhibitory role of RBM7 in breast cancer metastasis, we analyzed RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing data for RBM7 and whole-transcriptome sequencing data for breast cancer cells expressing two shRNAs targeting RBM7. Venn diagram of 8 hub genes obtained by overlapping three gene sets pointed forward a hotspot gene, namely MFGE8 (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by integrated analysis of multiple datasets shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The depletion of RBM7 resulted in a significant alteration in ratio of MFGE8 two isoforms.
source: RNA-seq data showed that the depletion of RBM7 resulted in a significant alteration in ratio of MFGE8 two isoforms, of which the canonical isoform (MFGE8-L) has been demonstrated to be correlated with tumor formation and aggressiveness of breast cancer (Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and citation to previous work on MFGE8-L function.

claim: The exon 7 located in F5/8 type C 2 domain was lacked in the short isoform of MFGE8 (MFGE8-S).
source: Importantly, the exon 7 located in F5/8 type C 2 domain, which is obligated to bind to phosphatidylserine, was lacked in the short isoform of MFGE8 (MFGE8-S) (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4B and knowledge about domain function.

claim: RBM7 ablation potentiated the production of MFGE8-S in various TNBC cell lines.
source: Further RT-PCR identification verified RBM7 ablation indeed potentiated the production of MFGE8-S in various TNBC cell lines (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR validation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The depletion of RBM7 induced the splicing shift of the MFGE8 minigene reporter by elevating MFGE8-S variant.
source: Accordingly, the depletion of RBM7 still induced the splicing shift of the minigene reporter by elevating MFGE8-S variant (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by minigene reporter assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Two poly(U) motifs are positioned in proximal to the pseudo 3' splice site of MFGE8 exon 7.
source: To test whether such splicing regulatory effect was directly or indirectly, we analyzed the sequence of alternative exon 7 and the motifs nearby its 5' or 3' splice sites, and found two poly(U) motifs are positioned in proximal to the pseudo 3' splice site.
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis of MFGE8 exon 7 and flanking regions.

claim: RBM7 could bind to the upstream sequence containing UUUCUU motifs adjacent to 3' splice site of MFGE8 cassette exon.
source: Subsequent RT-PCR assay for the precipitation in RIP assays confirmed RBM7 could bind to the upstream sequence containing UUUCUU motifs adjacent to 3' splice site of MFGE8 cassette exon, but not another region nearby it (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by RNA immunoprecipitation assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Treatment with ASOs targeting the potential binding site (UUUCUU) of RBM7 contributed to the exclusion of exon7 of MFGE8.
source: As shown in Figure 4F, when compared to control ASO, treatment with ASOs targeting the potential binding site (UUUCUU) of RBM7, contributed to the exclusion of exon7 of MFGE8.
evidence: Supported by antisense oligonucleotide experiment data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: RBM7 regulates the exon skipping of MFGE8 by directly binding to UUUCUU located at six nucleotides upstream of the 3' splice-site of exon7.
source: Oue data suggest that RBM7 regulates the exon skipping of MFGE8 by directly binding to UUUCUU located at six nucleotides upstream of the 3' splice-site of exon7.
evidence: Supported by integration of RIP, ASO, and minigene data, with inference about mechanism.

claim: MFGE8-L overexpression suppressed cellular migratory and invasive capabilities of breast cancer cells.
source: We applied MFGE8-L stably overexpressing- or depleted-breast cancer cells to transwell assays and observed the cellular migratory and invasive capabilities was visibly suppressed by MFGE8-L overexpression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: Supported by transwell assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: The knockdown of MFGE8-L provoked cell migration and invasion.
source: On the contrary, the knockdown of MFGE8-L provoked cell migration and invasion (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by transwell assay data with MFGE8-L knockdown shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: MFGE8-S not only totally abolished the inhibitory function of MFGE8-L but elicited modest pro-migration/invasion actions on breast cancer cells.
source: Strikingly, while MDA-MB-231 or HCC1937 expressing MFGE8-L showed a remarkable decrease in migratory and invasive ability compared to control vector, MFGE8-S not only totally abolished the inhibitory function of MFGE8-L but elicited modest pro-migration/ invasion actions on breast cancer cells (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-E).
evidence: Supported by transwell assay data comparing MFGE8-L and MFGE8-S shown in Figure 5A and supplementary figures.

claim: MFGE8-L up-regulation suppressed breast cancer cells invasion through a layer of extracellular matrix, whereas MFGE8-S enhanced ability to degrade matrix and invasion.
source: We also performed Fluorescent Gelatin Degradation Assays for investigating invadopodia formation and found MFGE8-L up-regulation suppressed breast cancer cells invasion through a layer of extracellular matrix, whereas breast cancer cells with ectopic expression of MFGE8-S acquired enhanced ability to degrade matrix and invasion (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by gelatin degradation assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: MFGE8-L forms foci in cytoplasm, particularly enriched near cell-cell contact sites, whereas MFGE8-S is more evenly distributed in the nucleus and cytoplasm.
source: Immunofluorescence assays revealed the MFGE8-L forms foci in cytoplasm, particularly enriched near cell-cell contact sites, whereas MFGE8-S is more evenly distributed in the nucleus and cytoplasm (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The protein encoded by MFGE8-S loses the second F5/8 type C domain, implying a shortage of the function corresponding to membrane-binding.
source: As shown in diagram of domain configuration for two variants, in comparison with MFGE8-L isoform containing N-terminal EGF-like domain and C-terminal twice-repeated F5/8 type C domains, the protein encoded by MFGE8-S loses the second F5/8 type C domain, implying a shortage of the function corresponding to membrane-binding (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by domain structure analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and inference about functional implications.

claim: A set of functional genes were down-regulated by MFGE8-L, whereas this negative regulation was abrogated in response to MFGE8-S.
source: Furthermore, we compared transcriptome profiles between MFGE8-L and MFGE8-S ectopically expressing breast cells and found a set of functional genes were down-regulated by MFGE8-L, whereas this negative regulation was abrogated in response to MFGE8-S (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by transcriptome profiling data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The differentially expressed genes between MFGE8-L and MFGE8-S were predominantly enriched in cell adhesion molecules and JAK-STAT cascade.
source: The differentially expressed genes between two splice variants were predominantly enriched in cell adhesion molecules and JAK-STAT cascade as revealed by KEGG pathway and Gene ontology analysis (Figure 5D and Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by KEGG pathway and Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: The activation of STAT1 was hindered by MFGE8-L, but not affected by MFGE8-S.
source: Subsequent experimental validation demonstrated that the activation of STAT1 was hindered by MFGE8-L, but not affected by MFGE8-S (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing STAT1 phosphorylation shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The restoration of MFGE8-L expression diminished the acquired aggressive properties of breast cancer cells resulted from RBM7 depletion.
source: Importantly, the restoration of MFGE8-L expression diminished the acquired aggressive properties of MDA-MB-231 cells resulted from RBM7 depletion (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The migrative and invasive ability of breast cancer cells treated with ASOs targeting RBM7-binding motif was significantly boosted.
source: The results showed an obvious increase in exon7-skipped variant as compared to the scramble negative control ASOs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B). Meanwhile, the migrative and invasive ability of breast cancer cells treated with ASOs was significantly boosted (Figure 6B), further suggesting that RBM7-knockdown stimulated aggressiveness of breast cancer at least partially relies on the control of MFGE8 AS.
evidence: Supported by ASO experiment data shown in Figure 6B and supplementary figure, with inference about mechanism.

claim: A series of shRBM7-upregulated secreted factors that have been reported to drive tumor angiogenesis were not impacted by MFGE8-L/S.
source: However, a series of shRBM7-upregulated secreted factors that have been reported to drive tumor angiogenesis (Gopinathan et al., 2015; Fousek et al., 2021; Feng et al., 2019), were not impacted by MFGE8-L/S (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6C and supplementary figure, with citations to previous work on angiogenesis factors.

claim: Condition medium derived from breast cancer cells overexpressing MFGE8-L/S showed negligible effect on HUVEC tube formation.
source: Condition medium derived from breast cancer cells overexpressing MFGE8-L/S showed negligible effect on HUVEC tube formation Figure 6—figure supplement 1D, implying that there exists additional mechanism underlying breast cancer metastasis attributed to RBM7 reduction.
evidence: Supported by tube formation assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and inference about additional mechanisms.

claim: Gene set enrichment analysis showed a signature for NF-κB pathway that was augmented upon depletion of RBM7.
source: Given that consecutive gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of highest-ranking gene sets based on transcriptomic profile of mRNA expression showed a signature for NF-κB pathway that was augmented upon depletion of RBM7 (Figure 6D), we suspected that the transcriptional activation of downstream genes in NF-κB signaling known to facilitate tumor angiogenesis might be involved in shRBM7-exerted pro-metastatic function.
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 6D and inference about mechanism.

claim: The phosphorylation of p65 was notably enhanced by RBM7 knockdown.
source: As expected, the phosphorylation of p65, a core transcription factor well-known to switch on NF-κB pathway, was notably enhanced by RBM7 knockdown. Meanwhile, IκBα phosphorylation that can blockade p65 activation was curbed upon RBM7 knockdown (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6E and knowledge about NF-κB pathway.

claim: RBM7 overexpression impeded the activation of p65.
source: Conversely, RBM7 overexpression impeded the activation of p65 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: MFGE8-L/S had no effect on phosphorylation of p65 or IκBα.
source: Yet MFGE8-L/S had no effect on phosphorylation of p65 or IκBα (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: RBM7 depletion remarkably promoted the expression of IL-1β.
source: We found RBM7 depletion remarkably promoted the expression of IL-1β as judged by qPCR and ELISA assays (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G-I).
evidence: Supported by qPCR and ELISA data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G-I.

claim: NF-κB inhibitor PDTC drastically reversed the promotion of HUVEC angiogenesis by conditional medium harvested from RBM7-depleted cells.
source: We further carried out Matrigel tube formation assays and found NF-κB inhibitor PDTC drastically reversed the promotion of HUVEC angiogenesis by conditional medium harvested from RBM7-depleted cells (Figure 6F–G), implying that RBM7-p65 axis may participate in HUVEC angiogenesis through reprogramming the secretome of breast cancer cells.
evidence: Supported by tube formation assay with NF-κB inhibitor shown in Figures 6F-G and inference about mechanism.

claim: Both MFGE8 splice switch and NF-κB pathway activation are required for mediating the pro-metastasis activity of RBM7 reduction in breast cancer.
source: Taken together, these data above indicated that both MFGE8 splice switch and NF-κB pathway activation are required for mediating the pro-metastasis activity of RBM7 reduction in breast cancer.
evidence: Supported by integration of multiple experimental results and inference about combined mechanisms.

claim: Exon7 skipping of MFGE8 occurs more frequently in tumor than in normal tissues in TCGA breast cancer cohort.
source: To study the clinical relevance of MFGE8 isoform switch, we analyzed the PSI changes of cassette exon7 in TCGA breast cancer cohort and found exon7 skipping occurs more frequently in tumor than in normal tissues (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The splicing of MFGE8 is shifted towards a reduced proportion of MFGE8-L across multiple cancer types, including LUAD, HNSC, COAD.
source: Consistently, in comparison with normal counterparts, the splicing of MFGE8 is shifted towards a reduced proportion of MFGE8-L across multiple cancer types, including LUAD, HNSC, COAD, etc (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by TCGA SpliceSeq data analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Increased proportion of exon7 exclusion was observed in most tumor samples when compared to normal tissues in breast cancer patients.
source: RT-PCR assay was performed in surgical tumor specimens in breast cancer patients and showed increased proportion of exon7 exclusion in most tumor samples when compared to normal tissues (case#1: 86:94; case#2: 84:86; case#3: 79:85; case#4: 63:75; case#5: 69:93; case#6: 71:80; Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data from patient samples shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The lymph node metastases contain a higher proportion of MFGE8 variant with skipped exon7 in comparison with paired primary tumor tissues.
source: On the other hand, the lymph node metastases contain a higher proportion of MFGE8 variant with skipped exon7 in comparison with paired primary tumor tissues (case#1: 80:95; case#2: 86:97; case#3: 84:90; case#4: 70:78; case#5: 83:89; Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data from paired patient samples shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Patients with high expression of MFGE8 exon7 had a visibly better overall survival than patients with low expression.
source: In addition, patients with high expression of MFGE8 exon7 had a visibly better overall survival than patients with low expression (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: There is a noticeably positive correlation between the expression of RBM7 and exon7 inclusion of MFGE8 in breast cancer.
source: We performed Pearson correlation test and revealed a noticeably positive correlation between the expression of RBM7 and exon7 inclusion of MFGE8 in breast cancer (Figure 7E), further supporting MFGE8 isoform switch regulated by RBM7.
evidence: Supported by Pearson correlation analysis shown in Figure 7E and inference about regulatory relationship.

claim: RBM7 could interact with RNA splicing factor SF3B2, a component of spliceosomal U2 SnRNP complex.
source: We performed co-IP experiment and found that RBM7 could interact with RNA splicing factor SF3B2, a component of spliceosomal U2 SnRNP complex (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and knowledge about SF3B2.

claim: The depletion of SF3B2 promoted exon7 skipping of MFGE8.
source: Consistent with the AS regulation of MFGE8 by RBM7, the depletion of SF3B2 also promoted exon7 skipping (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-D), implying a cooperative effect of the two proteins in regulating MFGE8 splicing.
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data with SF3B2 knockdown shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-D and inference about cooperative mechanism.

claim: RBM7 is commonly known to exert RNA surveillance activity as a component of the human nuclear exosome target (NEXT) complex.
source: RBM7, a member of RBP family, is commonly known to exert RNA surveillance activity as a component of the human nuclear exosome target (NEXT) complex (Meola et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on RBM7 function in NEXT complex.

claim: Aberrant expression of RBM7 is associated with lung fibrosis onset and motor neuronopathy.
source: Aberrant expression of RBM7 is not only associated with lung fibrosis onset and motor neuronopathy, but also impacts cancer cell proliferation (Fukushima et al., 2020; Xi et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on RBM7 in disease.

claim: RBM7 has been shown to directly connect with spliceosome factors SF3B2 and SF3B4.
source: Previous findings have established a direct connection of RBM7 with spliceosome factors SF3B2 and SF3B4 (Falk et al., 2016), yet whether RBM7 is involved in the regulation of AS remain elusive.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on RBM7 interactions.

claim: The canonical isoform MFGE8-L has been demonstrated to be correlated with tumor formation and aggressiveness of breast cancer.
source: RNA-seq data showed that the depletion of RBM7 resulted in a significant alteration in ratio of MFGE8 two isoforms, of which the canonical isoform (MFGE8-L) has been demonstrated to be correlated with tumor formation and aggressiveness of breast cancer (Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on MFGE8-L function.

claim: MFGE8 encodes a secreted protein that participates in mammary gland branching morphogenesis, angiogenesis, and mucosal healing.
source: MFGE8 encodes a secreted protein, Milk fat globule-EGF factor 8 (MFG-E8), which participates in a variety of cellular processes, including mammary gland branching morphogenesis, angiogenesis, and mucosal healing, etc (Raymond et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on MFGE8 function.

claim: STAT1 signaling activation plays an important role in tumor cell metastasis via cell adhesion molecules induction.
source: Considering that STAT1 signaling activation plays an important role in tumor cell metastasis via cell adhesion molecules induction (Marimuthu et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2019), it is highly plausible that MFGE8-L, but not MFGE8-S, impeded breast cancer cell motility and invasive capability in a STAT1-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on STAT1 in metastasis and inference about MFGE8 mechanism.

claim: IL-1β could bind to IL-1R and initiate a multistage enzymatic reaction that triggers the activation of NF-κB pathway.
source: IL-1β, commonly known as a pro-inflammatory cytokine, could bind to IL-1R and initiate a multistage enzymatic reaction that triggers the activation of NF-κB pathway (Weber et al., 2010; Guo et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on IL-1β signaling and knowledge about NF-κB activation.

claim: The upregulation of IL-1β might be a causal factor in RBM7-depletion-induced activation of NF-kB signaling.
source: IL-1β, commonly known as a pro-inflammatory cytokine, could bind to IL-1R and initiate a multistage enzymatic reaction that triggers the activation of NF-κB pathway (Weber et al., 2010; Guo et al., 2024). Thus, it is plausible the upregulation of IL-1β might be a causal factor in RBM7-depletion-induced activation of NF-kB signaling.
evidence: Inferred from IL-1β upregulation data and knowledge about IL-1β/NF-κB pathway.

claim: RBM7 mainly functions as a splicing activator in the context of SE/A5E in breast cancer.
source: Using whole-transcriptome sequencing, we found the depletion of RBM7 contributed to exon exclusion in approximately 70% SE/A5E events, implying RBM7 mainly functions as a splicing activator in the context of SE/A5E in breast cancer.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis and inference about RBM7 function.

claim: RRM domain of RBM7 could bind a proline-rich segment within SF3B2.
source: This is in concert with a previous study that RRM domain of RBM7 could bind a proline-rich segment within SF3B2 (Falk et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous structural study.

claim: The interaction mode indicates mutually exclusive binding of SF3B2 and ZCCHC8 to RBM7.
source: The interaction mode with strong similarity to RBM7RRM–ZCCHC8Proline interaction in the NEXT complex indicated mutually exclusive binding of SF3B2 and ZCCHC8 to RBM7.
evidence: Inferred from structural similarity to known RBM7-ZCCHC8 interaction.

claim: RBM7 appears to play dual, but not conflicting, roles during RNA processes depending on its interaction with the spliceosome or exosome.
source: Thus, RBM7 appears to play dual, but not conflicting, roles during RNA processes depending on its interaction with the spliceosome or exosome.
evidence: Inferred from evidence of RBM7 interactions with both splicing and exosome machinery.

claim: RBM7 shows decreased expression in breast cancer, particularly in the metastasis loci.
source: Nevertheless, in our study, RBM7 knockdown in breast cancer displayed visibly pro-metastasis function with activated NF-κB signaling. More importantly, according to TCGA database (total cases >1,000 used for analysis), RBM7 shows decreased expression in breast cancer, particularly in the metastasis loci and has positive correlation with patients' survival outcomes.
evidence: Supported by TCGA database analysis and experimental data.

claim: RBM7 has positive correlation with patients' survival outcomes.
source: More importantly, according to TCGA database (total cases >1,000 used for analysis), RBM7 shows decreased expression in breast cancer, particularly in the metastasis loci and has positive correlation with patients' survival outcomes.
evidence: Supported by TCGA database analysis.

claim: RBM7 regulated alternative splicing of AKT2, which is involved in glucose metabolism.
source: For example, we found RBM7 regulated alternative splicing of AKT2, which is involved in glucose metabolism (Hay, 2011).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and citation about AKT2 function.

claim: Down-regulated RBM7 and its cognate elevated exon7-exclusion MFGE8 were tightly related to enhanced breast cancer metastatic potential and poor prognosis of patients.
source: In conclusion, we discovered that down-regulated RBM7 and its cognate elevated exon7-exclusion MFGE8 were tightly related to enhanced breast cancer metastatic potential and poor prognosis of patients.
evidence: Supported by integration of clinical and experimental data throughout the study.

claim: MFGE8-L possessed the capability to trigger STAT1 phosphorylation and inhibit the motility and invasion of breast cancer cells.
source: MFGE8-L, the canonical variant, possessed the capability to trigger STAT1 phosphorylation and inhibit the motility and invasion of breast cancer cells, whereas splice switch to MFGE8-S was found loss-of-function for this tumor-suppressive role.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on STAT1 phosphorylation and cell migration/invasion assays.

claim: Splice switch to MFGE8-S was found loss-of-function for the tumor-suppressive role of MFGE8-L.
source: MFGE8-L, the canonical variant, possessed the capability to trigger STAT1 phosphorylation and inhibit the motility and invasion of breast cancer cells, whereas splice switch to MFGE8-S was found loss-of-function for this tumor-suppressive role.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing MFGE8-L and MFGE8-S effects.

claim: RBM7 reduction led to NF-κB pathway activation, resulting in enhancement of breast tumor aggressiveness.
source: At another layer, RBM7 reduction led to NF-κB pathway activation, resulting in enhancement of breast tumor aggressiveness.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on NF-κB signaling and tumor aggressiveness assays.

claim: Activated NF-κB pathway worked in concert with MFGE8 splicing transition to spur metastasis in RBM7-depleted breast cancer.
source: Overall, our findngs implicated that activated NF-κB pathway worked in concert with MFGE8 splicing transition to spur metastasis in RBM7-depleted breast cancer.
evidence: Inferred from integration of experimental results on both pathways.

claim: RBM7 and its regulated splicing variants might serve as potential therapeutic biomarker and prognostic indicator in breast cancer patients.
source: Additionally, although the detailed clinical significance underlying their cooperation need further in-depth investigation, we propose that RBM7 and its regulated splicing variants might serve as potential therapeutic biomarker and prognostic indicator in breast cancer patients.
evidence: Speculative proposal based on study findings about clinical correlations.

claim: Breast cancer is the most common diagnosed malignancy and remain the second leading cause of cancer mortality among females worldwide.
source: Breast cancer is the most common diagnosed malignancy and remain the second leading cause of cancer mortality (over 41,000 deaths annually in the USA) among females worldwide (Siegel et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to cancer statistics.

claim: Metastasis to vital organs accounts for approximately 90% cancer-related death.
source: Metastasis to vital organs accounts for approximately 90% cancer-related death.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about cancer mortality.

claim: The 5-year overall survival rate of patients with metastatic breast cancer is drastically decreased to about 25%, as compared to the primary cancer patients' prognosis with a survival rate greater than 80%.
source: The 5-year overall survival rate of patients with metastatic breast cancer is drastically decreased to about 25%, as compared to the primary cancer patients' prognosis with a survival rate greater than 80% (Rabbani and Mazar, 2007; Valastyan and Weinberg, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous clinical studies.

claim: Alternative splicing emerges as a substantial contributor to the production of a myriad of transcripts from limited genes.
source: Alternative splicing (AS) emerges as a substantial contributor to the production of a myriad of transcripts from limited genes, which enriched protein variation and phenotypic diversity in multicellular organisms.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about alternative splicing.

claim: Pre-mRNA splicing reactions require a step-wise assembly of spliceosome.
source: Pre-mRNA splicing reactions require a step-wise assembly of spliceosome, a megadalton complex that recognize consensus regulatory sequences, including 5' and 3' splice sites marking exon-intron boundary, and the branch point site (BPS), to accomplish exon definition (Shi, 2017; Wilkinson et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on splicing mechanisms.

claim: AS dysregulation leads to multiple human diseases, including cancer.
source: It is well documented that AS dysregulation leads to multiple human diseases, including cancer (Montes et al., 2019; Singh and Cooper, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on alternative splicing in disease.

claim: Splicing factors, particularly spliceosomal components SF3B1 and U2AF1, are frequently mutated across diverse cancer types.
source: In some cases, splicing factors, particularly spliceosomal components SF3B1 and U2AF1, are frequently mutated across diverse cancer types (Baralle and Baralle, 2005; Harbour et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2019; Cheruiyot et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on splicing factor mutations in cancer.

claim: Recurrent SF3B1 mutations led to retention of intronic region in BRD9 pre-mRNA, conferring loss of core subunit function to the ncBAF chromatin remodeling complex and metastatic advantage to melanoma cells.
source: For instance, recurrent SF3B1 mutations led to retention of intronic region in BRD9 pre-mRNA, conferring loss of core subunit function to the ncBAF chromatin remodeling complex and metastatic advantage to melanoma cells (Inoue et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on SF3B1 mutations.

claim: A set of members in SR protein family such as SRSF1 and SRSF3 are upregulated in breast tumors, lung tumors, glioma and exhibit oncogenic ability via altering AS products.
source: As an archetypal example, a set of members in SR protein family such as SRSF1 and SRSF3 are upregulated in breast tumors, lung tumors, glioma and exhibit oncogenic ability via altering AS products (for example, Bcl-x, MYO1B, NUMB, and p53; Anczuków et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2019; Tang et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on SR proteins in cancer.

claim: Many splicing factors such as RBM proteins can either functions as oncoproteins or tumor suppressors in cancer-type-dependent manner.
source: Otherwise, many splicing factors such as RBM (RNA binding motif) proteins can either functions as oncoproteins or tumor suppressors in cancer-type-dependent manner (Li et al., 2021), which may be attributed to tissue-specific AS patterns.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on RBM proteins and inference about tissue-specificity.

claim: The switch of CD44 or FGFR2 splicing isoforms can lead to EMT phenotype.
source: For example, the switch of CD44 or FGFR2 splicing isoforms can lead to EMT phenotype (Chen et al., 2018; Warzecha et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on splicing in EMT.

claim: VEGF-A or XBP1 splicing transition is tightly linked to angiogenesis in cancer.
source: VEGF-A or XBP1 splicing transition is tightly linked to angiogenesis in cancer (Harper and Bates, 2008; Zeng et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on splicing in angiogenesis.
